# How Thēseus got its accent back

The ASCII form *theseus* is missing something. **Thēseus** restores the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Greek evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the classification logic that separates Tier 1 restorations from Tier 2. By the end, the marks in Thēseus will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Thēseus
- **ASCII form:** theseus
- **Meaning:** "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)"
- **Domain of influence:** Heroism, Athens, Labours
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Θησεύς (Greek)
- **Live domain:** theseus.com

## Overview

**Thēseus** (*theseus*) — Heroism, Athens, Labours · The Gatherer (from τίθημι) — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Heroism, Athens, Labours". The name means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)".

**Thēseus** belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is associated with heroism, athens, labours.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Thēseus** and serves its temple at [theseus.com](https://punicodex.com/theseus/). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *theseus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Greek as **Θησεύς**. Etymologically it means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)".

The reconstructed proto-form is *dʰeh₁-* (proto-indo-european, "to put, to place"). Greek Θησεύς, popularly derived from τίθημι 'to set, to place'; the Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur and unified Attica.

The ASCII form *theseus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Thēseus** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Tau
- **h** → **h** — Theta
- **e** → **ē** — Eta: long epsilon
- **s** → **s** — Sigma
- **e** → **e** — Short epsilon
- **u** → **u** — Upsilon
- **s** → **s** — Sigma

The canonical temple for this name is served at **theseus.com**.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Greek as **Θησεύς**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *theseus* and the PuniCodex restoration **Thēseus** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'THESEUS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

## Mythology

The stories of **Thēseus** circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies heroism, athens, labours.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Thēseus is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with heroism, athens, labours.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Thēseus** is the Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur in the Cretan Labyrinth and unified Attica under Athens. With Ariadne's thread he navigated the maze, then abandoned her on Naxos—an act that later tradition both criticized and mythologized. His career bridges the age of monsters and the age of civic law. His later deeds—including the battle with the Centaurs, the Calydonian boar hunt, and the Amazonomachy—made him the paradigmatic civic hero of classical Athens.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Thēseus concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Thēseus carries the original marks of the Greek tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as Θησεύς.
- **Domain** — Heroism, Athens, Labours
- **Etymology** — The Gatherer (from τίθημι)

Thēseus is depicted as a **beardless young hero**, often with a **club**, a **sword**, or **Ariadne's thread**, and in scenes of the **Minotaur's defeat**. The Athenian ship with black sails, mistaken by Aegeus for a sign of death, is another recurring image.

His iconography deliberately rivals Herakles, asserting Attic pride.

## Epithets & Cult Titles

Thēseus is **Συνοικιστής** (*Synoikistēs*, founder of the synoikismos), **Ἡρακλείδης** (*Hērakleidēs*, rival of Herakles), and **Ποσειδῶνος παῖς** (*Poseidōnos pais*, son of Poseidon). Athenian oratory calls him **ὁ τῆς πόλεως κτίστης** (*ho tēs poleōs ktistēs*, founder of the city).

Each title reflects a different civic identity: unifier, hero, and divine son.

## The Homeric Hymns

The **Odyssey** places **Thēseus** in the underworld alongside Pirithous, punished for the attempt to abduct Persephone. The **Homeric Hymn to Apollo** presupposes Attic hero-cult and may reflect the Theseid tradition, though Theseus himself is not hymned.

His labours and synoikismos made him the Attic equivalent of Herakles, a figure too human for an Olympian hymn yet too heroic for ordinary mortality.

## Oracle Sites & Sanctuaries

Thēseus consulted **Apollo at Delphi** before his journey to Crete; the oracle told him to take Aphrodite as his guide, which led him to choose Ariadne. His bones were later brought from Skyros to Athens on Delphic advice, cementing the link between hero and sanctuary.

Delphi thus guided both his departure and his posthumous return.

Thēseus continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes. Theseus became the symbolic founder of Athenian democracy and a recurring figure in classical tragedy, Renaissance painting, and modern retellings of the Minotaur myth.

## The Unicode Restoration

Thēseus is classified as **Tier 1**: the original carries both stress and length, and only one valid Unicode restoration exists. The ASCII fallback *theseus* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 7 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 mark of length (ē). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **theseus.com**. Behind the scenes the DNS carries it in punycode form — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Thēseus; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Greek can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Thēseus**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *theseus* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 7 characters, 6 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **t** stays as it is — Tau.

The **h** stays as it is — Theta.

The **e** becomes **ē** — Eta: long epsilon.

The **s** stays as it is — Sigma.

The **e** stays as it is — Short epsilon.

The **u** stays as it is — Upsilon.

The **s** stays as it is — Sigma.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
